content: 1. For adults undergoing dental procedures, the preferred oral antibiotic prophylaxis regimen is a single dose of 2 grams of amoxicillin administered 30 to 60 minutes prior to the procedure. For pediatric patients, the dose is 50 mg/kg, also given as a single dose 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure. 2. If oral medication cannot be taken, the preferred regimen for adults is a single dose of 2 grams of ampicillin intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV), 1 gram of cefazolin IM or IV, or 1 gram of ceftriaxone IM or IV, all administered 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure. For pediatric patients, the dose is 50 mg/kg of ampicillin, cefazolin, or ceftriaxone. 3. For patients allergic to penicillins or ampicillin, the preferred oral regimen includes a single dose of 2 grams of cephalexin, 600 mg of clindamycin, 500 mg of azithromycin, or 500 mg of clarithromycin, all administered 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure. For pediatric patients, the doses are 50 mg/kg of cephalexin, 20 mg/kg of clindamycin, or 15 mg/kg of azithromycin or clarithromycin. 4. For patients allergic to penicillins or ampicillin and unable to take oral medication, the preferred regimen includes a single dose of 1 gram of cefazolin IM or IV, 1 gram of ceftriaxone IM or IV, or 600 mg of clindamycin IM or IV, all administered 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure. For pediatric patients, the doses are 50 mg/kg of cefazolin or ceftriaxone, or 20 mg/kg of clindamycin. 5. Antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent infective endocarditis (IE) is no longer recommended for patients undergoing gastrointestinal (GI) or genitourinary (GU) tract procedures. 6. For respiratory tract procedures, the preferred oral regimen for adults is a single dose of 2 grams of amoxicillin administered 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure. For pediatric patients, the dose is 50 mg/kg, also given as a single dose 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure. 7. If oral medication cannot be taken for respiratory tract procedures, the preferred regimen for adults is a single dose of 2 grams of ampicillin IM or IV, 1 gram of cefazolin IM or IV, or 1 gram of ceftriaxone IM or IV, all administered 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure. For pediatric patients, the dose is 50 mg/kg of ampicillin, cefazolin, or ceftriaxone. 8. For patients allergic to penicillins or ampicillin undergoing respiratory tract procedures, the preferred oral regimen includes a single dose of 2 grams of cephalexin, 600 mg of clindamycin, 500 mg of azithromycin, or 500 mg of clarithromycin, all administered 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure. For pediatric patients, the doses are 50 mg/kg of cephalexin, 20 mg/kg of clindamycin, or 15 mg/kg of azithromycin or clarithromycin. 9. For patients allergic to penicillins or ampicillin and unable to take oral medication for respiratory tract procedures, the preferred regimen includes a single dose of 1 gram of cefazolin IM or IV, 1 gram of ceftriaxone IM or IV, or 600 mg of clindamycin IM or IV, all administered 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure. For pediatric patients, the doses are 50 mg/kg of cefazolin or ceftriaxone, or 20 mg/kg of clindamycin. 10. For procedures involving infected skin, skin structures, or musculoskeletal tissue, it is reasonable to include an agent active against staphylococci and beta-hemolytic streptococci, such as an antistaphylococcal penicillin or a cephalosporin, as part of the therapeutic regimen for treating the infection. 11. Infectious aortitis is caused by pathogens such as Salmonella, Staphylococcus aureus, Group A streptococcus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Escherichia coli or other Gram-negative bacilli, and fungi. Antimicrobial treatment should include bactericidal, broad-spectrum agents administered after obtaining blood cultures and prior to surgery. Therapy should be adjusted based on culture results. Examples include ceftriaxone 2 grams IV every 4–6 hours for 6–12 weeks or vancomycin 1 gram IV every 12 hours for 6–12 weeks. 12. For cardiovascular implantable electronic device (CIED) infections with complicated generator pocket infections, systemic signs of infection, or positive blood cultures, treatment should follow protocols for lead or endocardial involvement. For CIED-associated native or prosthetic valve endocarditis (CIED-IE), Duke criteria for definite endocarditis should be met, including echocardiographic evidence of valve involvement. 13. For CIED infections where device removal is not required or feasible, prolonged therapy post-removal is generally unnecessary. However, for CIED-IE or CIED lead infections (CIED-LI) where extraction is too risky or declined, and the device is absolutely required, six weeks of IV therapy is recommended. 14. For CIED infections with negative blood cultures, the preferred regimen includes vancomycin 1 gram IV every 12 hours or daptomycin 8–10 mg/kg IV every 24 hours, combined with gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV every 12 hours. Antimicrobial therapy should be selected based on the identification and susceptibility of the infecting pathogen. 15. Alternative regimens for Gram-negative bacteria may include cefepime, imipenem-cilastatin, meropenem, or ertapenem. Daptomycin may be considered as a substitute for vancomycin in certain cases.
